prompt: A friend asks whether you liked the business plan they emailed you. You found serious problems in it, and a quick 'It's great!' would be much easier. What does Ephesians 4:25 counsel here?
options: Tell them it is perfect so you avoid an awkward conversation
Speak the truth to them, because you are members one of another
Say nothing and simply stop replying to their messages
Praise it to their face but tell others what you really think
explanation: Ephesians 4:25 says, "putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another." Honest speech, not a convenient falsehood, is the instruction.
hint: The verse gives a reason for honesty based on how believers are joined together.
kjv: Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
r1_problems: The marked answer adds 'kindly', which is not in Ephesians 4:25. The idea of speaking the truth in love comes from 4:15, not the cited verse. It is a minor addition, but the marked response should reflect only what the cited verse teaches. Everything else is sound: the distractors clearly contradict the command to put away lying and speak truth.

prompt: Months ago, during a moving worship service, you made a sincere vow to God to give a specific gift to a ministry. Since then you keep putting it off, half-wondering whether a vow made in the moment really counts. What does Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 counsel?
options: Fulfil what you vowed without delay, since it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay
Consider the vow cancelled because it was made in an emotional moment
Keep postponing indefinitely, since God does not mind delays
Make a larger vow to make up for the unpaid one
explanation: Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 says, "When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it... Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay." A vow should be kept, and kept promptly.
hint: The passage speaks both about timing and about whether vowing at all is wise.
kjv: When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
r1_problems: The marked answer matches the text exactly, and the distractors are clearly contrary. However, the scenario says 'money is tighter', so the item reads like telling someone in financial strain to hand over money anyway. That edges into financial pressure or advice and could come across as heavy-handed. Removing the hardship framing keeps the point (do not defer a vow) without that concern.

prompt: You and your spouse had a heated disagreement about household chores this evening. It is getting late, and you are tempted to go to bed still fuming and deal with it 'some other time.' What does Ephesians 4:26 counsel here?
options: Let the anger simmer for a few days so your spouse learns a lesson
Deal with the anger without sinning and seek to settle it before the day ends
Say nothing, but quietly keep holding on to your resentment
Vent to friends over the next few days while staying angry at your spouse
keywords: sun go down upon your wrath
explanation: Ephesians 4:26 says, 'Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath.' Anger is not to lead to sin, nor to be carried past the end of the day. It should be dealt with promptly rather than nursed.
hint: Think about what the verse says regarding the end of the day.
kjv: Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
r1_problems: Two distractors are not clearly contrary to the verse as worded. Ephesians 4:26 is about not harbouring wrath past sundown, not specifically about discussing things with the spouse or avoiding friends. Options C and D should explicitly involve continuing to nurse the anger.

prompt: You have a flexible remote job and no manager checking in daily. It's tempting to coast through the slow season and scramble later when the busy months arrive. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 6:6-8?
options: Relax fully now, since nobody is watching and the busy season is far off
Work steadily and prepare during the slow season, without needing someone to oversee you
Do only what is checked, because effort without a supervisor is wasted
Wait until the busy season starts and then decide how to cope
explanation: Proverbs 6:6-8 points the sluggard to the ant, which has "no guide, overseer, or ruler" yet "provideth her meat in the summer." Diligence and preparation should not depend on being supervised.
hint: Think of a small creature that gathers its food in summer and harvest with no one telling it to.
kjv: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.
r1_problems: The hint says the ant gathers food 'before winter'. Proverbs 6:6-8 does not mention winter; it says only that the ant provides in the summer and gathers in the harvest. This is a minor addition to the text. The rest of the item is accurate: the marked answer matches the passage and the other options clearly contradict it.

prompt: You're excited about a major home renovation and want to start knocking down walls this weekend. You haven't yet worked out whether you have the money to finish it. Which response best reflects Jesus' teaching in Luke 14:28-30?
options: Start right away; enthusiasm will carry the project to completion
Begin the demolition and figure out the budget once you see how it goes
Avoid all large projects, since any plan might fail
Sit down first and count the cost to see if you can finish what you start
explanation: In Luke 14:28-30 Jesus asks, "which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?" Otherwise onlookers would mock the one who "began to build, and was not able to finish." Jesus gives this picture to illustrate counting the cost of following him, and the principle is to count the cost before starting.
hint: Jesus describes someone building a tower and what he does before laying the foundation.
kjv: For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.
r1_problems: The explanation misquotes the passage. It says the builder "sitteth not down first," which reads as if the builder fails to sit down. In the KJV this phrase is part of a rhetorical question ("which of you... sitteth not down first"), meaning everyone would sit down first. The explanation should present it as a question. Minor point: in context Jesus uses the illustration about the cost of discipleship, but applying its plain principle of counting the cost before building is a fair application.

prompt: Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, and wise men from the east came to Jerusalem seeking him. Which marker shows Bethlehem?
explanation: Matthew 2:1 records that Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, and that wise men came from the east to Jerusalem.
hint: Look in the hill country of Judea, just south of Jerusalem.
kjv: Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem,
options: A
B
C
D
r1_problems: The prompt says the wise men came to Bethlehem seeking him, but the cited verse (Matthew 2:1) says they came 'to Jerusalem'. They reach Bethlehem only later, in 2:9–11. The wording should match the cited text.

prompt: When the ark of God was sent to the city marked on the map, its people cried out that it had been brought to slay them. Which city is it?
explanation: The Philistines sent the ark of God to Ekron, and the Ekronites cried out in fear (1 Samuel 5:10).
hint: After Ashdod and Gath, the ark was sent on to this city, whose people feared it would kill them.
kjv: Therefore they sent the ark of God to Ekron. And it came to pass, as the ark of God came to Ekron, that the Ekronites cried out, saying, They have brought about the ark of the God of Israel to us, to slay us and our people.
options: Ekron
Bethel
Shechem
Hazor
r1_problems: The hint claims Ekron was the Philistine city 'closest to the hill country of Judah'. This geographic claim is not supported by the cited text and is debatable, since Gath could be argued to lie closer. The 'last stop' claim is accurate per 1 Samuel 5–6, but it rests on context beyond the cited verse. The hint also names the city as Philistine, and none of the distractors is a Philistine city, so the item becomes very easy.

prompt: The king of the city marked on the map sent his servants unto Solomon when he heard Solomon had been anointed king, for this king was ever a lover of David. Which city is it?
explanation: Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants unto Solomon, having heard he was anointed king in his father's room, for Hiram was ever a lover of David (1 Kings 5:1).
hint: A famous Phoenician seaport north of Israel.
kjv: And Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants unto Solomon; for he had heard that they had anointed him king in the room of his father: for Hiram was ever a lover of David.
options: Tyre
Joppa
Gaza
Beersheba
r1_problems: The cited verse (1 Kings 5:1) says only that Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon. It does not mention cedar; the cedar supply comes in 1 Kings 5:6-10. The prompt therefore adds detail that the cited text does not support.

prompt: Fleeing the Philistines, the men of Israel fell down slain on the mountain marked on the map, and the Philistines slew Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua. Which mountain is it?
explanation: The men of Israel fled from the Philistines and fell down slain in mount Gilboa, and the Philistines slew Saul's sons (1 Samuel 31:1-2).
hint: It rises above the Jezreel valley's eastern end.
kjv: Now the Philistines fought against Israel: and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines, and fell down slain in mount Gilboa. And the Philistines followed hard upon Saul and upon his sons; and the Philistines slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchi-shua, Saul’s sons.
options: Mount Gilboa
Mount Tabor
Mount Carmel
Mount Hermon
r1_problems: The prompt says this is where Saul died, but the cited verses (1 Samuel 31:1-2) only record Israel's men falling slain in mount Gilboa and the Philistines killing Saul's sons. Saul's own death comes in verses 3-6 and is placed in Gilboa in verse 8. The prompt should match the cited text.

prompt: In Abram's day, kings were joined together in the vale of Siddim, 'which is the salt sea.' Which marker shows the Salt Sea?
explanation: Genesis 14:3 says the kings were joined together in the vale of Siddim, which is the salt sea.
hint: It lies at the southern end of the Jordan River.
kjv: All these were joined together in the vale of Siddim, which is the salt sea.
options: A
B
C
D
r1_problems: The prompt says the kings 'joined battle,' a phrase from Genesis 14:8. The cited verse, Genesis 14:3, says they 'were joined together.' This is a minor mismatch with the cited text. Otherwise the item is accurate.

prompt: King Omri bought a hill from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city on it, naming it Samaria. Which marker shows Samaria?
explanation: 1 Kings 16:24 tells how Omri 'bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver' and called the city Samaria 'after the name of Shemer, owner of the hill.' It became the capital of the northern kingdom.
hint: It was the northern kingdom's capital, in the hill country north of Jerusalem.
kjv: And he bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver, and built on the hill, and called the name of the city which he built, after the name of Shemer, owner of the hill, Samaria.
options: A
B
C
D
r1_problems: In the explanation, 'named the city after him' is ambiguous because 'him' could be read as Omri. The verse says the city was named after Shemer, the owner of the hill. The note that Samaria became the northern capital is background, not stated in this verse, but it is accurate.

case_title: The Silver Cup in the Sack
briefing: Eleven brothers set out for home from Egypt with full sacks of corn, and a costly silver cup goes missing from the house of the ruler. Your case file is Genesis 44: trace how the cup got into the sack, how it was found, and how the matter was settled.
clue: Witness statement: 'We were gone out of the city, and not yet far off, when the steward overtook us and put a hard question to us.'
prompt: What question did Joseph tell the steward to put to the men when he overtook them?
options: Wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good?
Why have ye not paid for your corn?
Where is your youngest brother?
Why did ye leave before morning?
explanation: Joseph instructed the steward to say, 'Wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good?' and to describe the cup as the one in which his lord drinks and divines (Genesis 44:4-5).
hint: The question contrasts two opposites: what they received and what they gave back.
kjv: And when they were gone out of the city, and not yet far off, Joseph said unto his steward, Up, follow after the men; and when thou dost overtake them, say unto them, Wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good? Is not this it in which my lord drinketh, and whereby indeed he divineth? ye have done evil in so doing.
r1_problems: The clue mixes pronouns ('They were out of the city... caught up with us'), which makes the witness statement confusing. Otherwise the question, answer, hint and explanation match Genesis 44:4-5.

case_title: The Silver Cup in the Sack
briefing: Eleven brothers set out for home from Egypt with full sacks of corn, and a costly silver cup goes missing from the house of the ruler. Your case file is Genesis 44: trace how the cup got into the sack, how it was found, and how the matter was settled.
clue: Household record: the master of the house gave orders to his steward about the travellers' sacks, including special instructions about his own cup.
prompt: According to the text, who ordered the silver cup to be put in the youngest brother's sack?
options: Joseph, who commanded his steward to do it
Benjamin, who hid it there himself
Judah, who wanted to test his brothers
Reuben, who took it from the table
explanation: Joseph commanded his steward to put 'my cup, the silver cup, in the sack's mouth of the youngest,' and the steward 'did according to the word that Joseph had spoken' (Genesis 44:1-2).
hint: Read who 'commanded the steward of his house.'
kjv: And he commanded the steward of his house, saying, Fill the men’s sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put every man’s money in his sack’s mouth. And put my cup, the silver cup, in the sack’s mouth of the youngest, and his corn money. And he did according to the word that Joseph had spoken.
r1_problems: The clue says the orders were given 'before dawn' and were 'private.' Genesis 44:1-2 gives neither the timing nor any secrecy. Verse 3 says only that the men were sent away 'as soon as the morning was light,' so the clue adds details Scripture does not state. The question, options, answer, explanation and hint are otherwise sound.

briefing: Samson, the judge of Israel, has broken every bond his enemies placed on him, and no one knows why he cannot be overpowered. In Judges 16 a woman is offered a fortune to uncover his secret. Your task is to follow the evidence, stage by stage, to learn how the strongest man in Israel was finally brought low.
clue: Intercepted message: Powerful men came up unto Delilah with a proposal and a price for her cooperation.
prompt: Who approached Delilah, and what did each of them promise her?
options: The priests of Dagon, each promising a talent of gold
The lords of the Philistines, each promising eleven hundred pieces of silver
Samson's father and mother, each promising a flock of sheep
The men of Judah, each promising thirty changes of garments
explanation: In Judges 16:5 the lords of the Philistines asked Delilah to entice Samson and promised, "every one of us eleven hundred pieces of silver."
hint: The offer was made in silver, and it came from Israel's enemies.
kjv: And the lords of the Philistines came up unto her, and said unto her, Entice him, and see wherein his great strength lieth, and by what means we may prevail against him, that we may bind him to afflict him: and we will give thee every one of us eleven hundred pieces of silver.
r1_problems: Minor: the clue says the men came 'to Delilah's house', but Judges 16:5 says only that they 'came up unto her'. A dwelling is implied later by the chamber in 16:9, but the clue should not add the location. The answer, options, explanation and hint are accurate.

briefing: Samson, the judge of Israel, has broken every bond his enemies placed on him, and no one knows why he cannot be overpowered. In Judges 16 a woman is offered a fortune to uncover his secret. Your task is to follow the evidence, stage by stage, to learn how the strongest man in Israel was finally brought low.
clue: Evidence bag #1: Seven fresh, undried withs recovered from Delilah's chamber, where men had been lying in wait. Samson broke them as a thread of tow breaks when it touches the fire.
prompt: When Delilah first asked, what did Samson say would make him weak?
options: Being bound with chains of iron
Having his eyes put out
Being bound with seven green withs that were never dried
Being kept from eating bread and drinking water
explanation: Samson told Delilah, "If they bind me with seven green withs that were never dried, then shall I be weak" (Judges 16:7), yet he broke them when she bound him (Judges 16:9).
hint: Look for something freshly cut that had not yet dried out.
kjv: And Delilah said to Samson, Tell me, I pray thee, wherein thy great strength lieth, and wherewith thou mightest be bound to afflict thee. And Samson said unto her, If they bind me with seven green withs that were never dried, then shall I be weak, and be as another man. Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven green withs which had not been dried, and she bound him with them. Now there were men lying in wait, abiding with her in the chamber. And she said unto him, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And he brake the withs, as a thread of tow is broken when it toucheth the fire. So his strength was not known.
r1_problems: The clue says the cords were found 'near the room' and implies the Philistines were somewhere nearby. Verse 9 says the men were lying in wait 'abiding with her in the chamber', and Samson was bound with the withs in that chamber. The location detail is not in the text and is slightly inaccurate. The question, options, answer, explanation and hint are all sound.

briefing: Samson, the judge of Israel, has broken every bond his enemies placed on him, and no one knows why he cannot be overpowered. In Judges 16 a woman is offered a fortune to uncover his secret. Your task is to follow the evidence, stage by stage, to learn how the strongest man in Israel was finally brought low.
clue: Final report: Delilah cried, "The Philistines be upon thee, Samson." He awoke and said he would go out as at other times before and shake himself. The text adds that he did not know something had changed.
prompt: What really happened that left Samson powerless?
options: Delilah bound him with new ropes while the Philistines held him down
He was wounded in battle and carried to Gaza
While he slept upon Delilah's knees, a man shaved off the seven locks of his head, and his strength went from him
The lords of the Philistines put out his eyes before he could escape
explanation: Judges 16:19 says Delilah "made him sleep upon her knees" and had a man "shave off the seven locks of his head," and "his strength went from him"; verse 20 adds that "he wist not that the LORD was departed from him."
hint: Remember the secret he revealed in the previous stage, and what happened while he slept.
kjv: And she made him sleep upon her knees; and she called for a man, and she caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head; and she began to afflict him, and his strength went from him. And she said, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And he awoke out of his sleep, and said, I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself. And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.
r1_problems: The clue says 'this time the Philistines took him,' but that comes from Judges 16:21, which is outside the cited reference (16:19-20). It is scripturally accurate, but the clue should stay within the cited text. Everything else is accurate. Option D (putting out his eyes) happens after his capture in v21, so it cannot be defended as the cause.

briefing: Two strangers from the camp of Israel slipped into Jericho, and by nightfall the king's men were knocking at a house on the town wall. Your case file is Joshua 2: follow the evidence in story order to learn who sent the men, where they vanished, and how they escaped the city.
clue: Gatekeeper's report: the king's men went out in pursuit of the spies, and as soon as the pursuers had gone out, the city gate was shut behind them.
prompt: Which way did the pursuers go in search of the men?
options: The way to Jordan unto the fords
Toward the Red sea
Back to Shittim
North to the mountain of Lebanon
explanation: Joshua 2:7 records that the men pursued after them the way to Jordan unto the fords, and the gate was shut once they had gone out.
hint: The pursuers headed toward a river crossing.
kjv: And the men pursued after them the way to Jordan unto the fords: and as soon as they which pursued after them were gone out, they shut the gate.
r1_problems: The clue says the king's men 'rode out', which implies horses or chariots; Joshua 2:7 says only that they 'pursued' and 'were gone out'. The 'gatekeeper's report' framing is acceptable, but the riding detail should be removed.

briefing: In 1 Kings 3, two women stand before King Solomon with one living baby and one dead one, and each claims the living child as her own. There were no other witnesses in the house, so the king must uncover the truth from their testimony alone. Gather the evidence and discover how the true mother was revealed.
clue: Witness statement: "She arose at midnight... while thine handmaid slept." At morning, the first woman examined the dead child closely.
prompt: What did the first woman claim happened at midnight?
options: The other woman fled the house with both babies
A servant switched the children
The other woman took her son and laid her own dead child in the first woman's bosom
She woke and found both babies missing
explanation: She said the other woman "took my son from beside me... and laid her dead child in my bosom," and in the morning she saw "it was not my son, which I did bear" (1 Kings 3:20-21).
hint: Think about what was exchanged while she slept.
kjv: And she arose at midnight, and took my son from beside me, while thine handmaid slept, and laid it in her bosom, and laid her dead child in my bosom. And when I rose in the morning to give my child suck, behold, it was dead: but when I had considered it in the morning, behold, it was not my son, which I did bear.
r1_problems: The correct option's pronouns are ambiguous. In "took her son and laid her dead child in her bosom," the final "her" could be read as the other woman's own bosom. The KJV says she laid the dead child "in my bosom," meaning the first woman's. Rewording makes clear the dead child was placed with the first woman. Everything else is accurate: the clue, the briefing (v.18: "no stranger with us in the house, save we two"), the explanation and the hint.

briefing: Two strangers from the camp of Israel slipped into Jericho, and by nightfall the king's men were knocking at a house on the town wall. Your case file is Joshua 2: follow the evidence in story order to learn who sent the men, where they vanished, and how they escaped the city.
clue: Statement given to the king's messengers: 'There came men unto me, but I wist not whence they were... pursue after them quickly.' Yet the text says she had already taken the two men and hid them.
prompt: Where were the two men actually hidden?
options: On the roof, under stalks of flax
In a cave outside the city
In the king's own storehouse
At the bottom of a well
explanation: Joshua 2:6 says she had brought them up to the roof of the house and hid them with the stalks of flax which she had laid in order upon the roof.
hint: Think high, not low, and of something she had laid out in order there.
kjv: And the woman took the two men, and hid them, and said thus, There came men unto me, but I wist not whence they were: And it came to pass about the time of shutting of the gate, when it was dark, that the men went out: whither the men went I wot not: pursue after them quickly; for ye shall overtake them. But she had brought them up to the roof of the house, and hid them with the stalks of flax, which she had laid in order upon the roof.
r1_problems: The clue adds an unsupported detail: 'Yet the searchers found no one in the house.' Joshua 2:4-6 (and 2:7) never says the king's messengers searched the house. It says only that she gave her statement and that they then pursued toward Jordan. The answer, options, explanation and hint are otherwise sound. 'Under stalks of flax' is an acceptable paraphrase of 'hid them with the stalks of flax.'

briefing: Jacob has left Paddan-aram with his wives, children and flocks, and Laban has discovered that his household images are gone. Working only from Genesis 31, piece together when they vanished, how Laban gave chase, what was said, and where the missing gods really were.
clue: Messenger's report: word of Jacob's flight reached Laban late, and he set out with his brethren on a long pursuit.
prompt: Where did Laban and his brethren overtake Jacob?
options: At the brook Jabbok
In the mount Gilead
At the well of Bethel
At the gates of Shechem
explanation: Laban was told on the third day that Jacob had fled, pursued him seven days' journey, and overtook him in the mount Gilead (Genesis 31:22-23).
hint: After seven days' journey, Laban caught up with Jacob in a mountain region.
kjv: And it was told Laban on the third day that Jacob was fled. And he took his brethren with him, and pursued after him seven days’ journey; and they overtook him in the mount Gilead. And God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream by night, and said unto him, Take heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad.
r1_problems: The hint relies on Genesis 31:21 (Jacob 'set his face toward the mount Gilead'), which is accurate KJV but outside the cited reference 31:22-24. The hint should be grounded in the cited verses. The clue's word 'late' is a mild paraphrase of 'on the third day' and is acceptable.

briefing: Jacob has left Paddan-aram with his wives, children and flocks, and Laban has discovered that his household images are gone. Working only from Genesis 31, piece together when they vanished, how Laban gave chase, what was said, and where the missing gods really were.
clue: Search record: Laban went from tent to tent through the camp, finding nothing in the first several he entered.
prompt: After searching Jacob's tent, Leah's tent and the two maidservants' tents without finding the images, which tent did Laban enter next?
options: Jacob's tent
The two maidservants' tents
Rachel's tent
Laban's own tent
explanation: Laban searched Jacob's tent, Leah's tent and the two maidservants' tents without finding the gods, then went out of Leah's tent and entered into Rachel's tent (Genesis 31:33).
hint: One wife's tent had not yet been searched.
kjv: And Laban went into Jacob’s tent, and into Leah’s tent, and into the two maidservants’ tents; but he found them not. Then went he out of Leah’s tent, and entered into Rachel’s tent.
r1_problems: The prompt 'after leaving Leah's tent' clashes with the order of the list in the verse, where the maidservants' tents come after Leah's. That makes the maidservants' option arguable. Rewording the prompt to follow the full search sequence removes the ambiguity.

briefing: A grieving father in Canaan holds a torn, blood-soaked garment and believes his favoured son is dead. Your assignment is to trace the coat's journey from Jacob's tent to the wilderness pit and uncover what really happened, using only the testimony of Genesis 37.
clue: Evidence item #1: A coat of many colours, made by the father for the one son he loved more than all his brethren.
prompt: According to the text, why did Israel love Joseph more than all his children and make him this coat?
options: Because Joseph was the son of his old age
Because Joseph was the firstborn son
Because Joseph had saved the family flocks
Because Joseph had been chosen by the elders
explanation: Genesis 37:3 says Israel loved Joseph more than all his children 'because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours.' Genesis 37:4 adds that his brothers hated him for this favour.
hint: Think about Joseph's age compared with his father's age when he was born.
kjv: Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours. And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him.
r1_problems: The clue adds details the text does not give. Genesis 37:3 says 'a coat of many colours', not a 'richly made garment'. It never says the coat was 'unlike anything the other brothers wear'. The 'witnesses' testimony that it went to only one son is also inference, not stated in the passage. The question, options, answer, explanation and hint are sound.

briefing: After the stunning fall of Jericho, Israel suffers an unexpected and humiliating defeat at the small city of Ai. Something has gone terribly wrong in the camp, and the LORD reveals that a hidden wrong must be uncovered before Israel can stand again. Investigate the case of 'The Hidden Plunder' in Joshua 7.
clue: Field report from Ai: On the spies' advice that the men of Ai were but few, about three thousand men went up, yet they were chased from before the gate and some were smitten, and the hearts of the people melted, and became as water.
prompt: What happened to the Israelite force that went up against Ai?
options: They fled before the men of Ai, who smote about thirty and six of them
They captured Ai without losing a single man
They besieged Ai for seven days until its walls fell
They made a peace treaty with the king of Ai
keywords: fled before the men of Ai
explanation: About three thousand men went up, but they fled before the men of Ai, who smote about thirty and six of them, and the people's hearts melted (Joshua 7:4-5).
hint: The report speaks of retreat and losses, not victory.
kjv: And Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is beside Beth-aven, on the east side of Beth-el, and spake unto them, saying, Go up and view the country. And the men went up and viewed Ai. And they returned to Joshua, and said unto him, Let not all the people go up; but let about two or three thousand men go up and smite Ai; and make not all the people to labour thither; for they are but few. So there went up thither of the people about three thousand men: and they fled before the men of Ai. And the men of Ai smote of them about thirty and six men: for they chased them from before the gate even unto Shebarim, and smote them in the going down: wherefore the hearts of the people melted, and became as water.
r1_problems: The clue says the men 'went up confidently.' The text records only the spies' advice that a small force would be enough ('they are but few'). It never describes the soldiers' confidence, so this adds an inference. The hint also says the report speaks of casualties, but the clue mentions none.

briefing: During a royal banquet in Babylon, a disembodied hand writes a message on the palace wall, and the king's wise men cannot explain it. Your task is to work through the case file in Daniel 5 and find out what the writing meant and what happened that same night.
clue: Evidence from the banquet hall: at a great feast for a thousand lords, the king commanded that certain golden and silver vessels be brought in, and he, his princes, his wives and his concubines drank wine from them.
prompt: According to the record, where had the vessels used at Belshazzar's feast come from?
options: The temple of the house of God at Jerusalem, taken by Nebuchadnezzar
The treasury of the Medes and Persians, received as tribute
The royal workshops of Babylon, made for this feast
The temple of Bel, brought in by the Chaldean priests
explanation: Belshazzar ordered the golden and silver vessels that his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple in Jerusalem, and the guests drank from them while praising gods of gold, silver, brass, iron, wood and stone (Daniel 5:1-4).
hint: The text names the city these cups were taken from and the king who took them.
kjv: Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand. Belshazzar, whiles he tasted the wine, commanded to bring the golden and silver vessels which his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple which was in Jerusalem; that the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, might drink therein. Then they brought the golden vessels that were taken out of the temple of the house of God which was at Jerusalem; and the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, drank in them. They drank wine, and praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone.
r1_problems: The clue invents a detail Scripture does not give: a servant reporting that the cups were not made for the palace. Daniel 5:1-4 mentions no such servant or report. The clue also slightly misstates the scene: Belshazzar 'drank wine before the thousand', and the drinkers from the vessels were the king, his princes, wives and concubines. The question, options, answer, explanation and hint are accurate.

briefing: In the early Jerusalem church, a couple sold a possession and brought money to the apostles, but within hours both were dead and fear had spread through the whole church. Your case file covers Acts 5:1-11. Follow the money, the words spoken, and the timeline to learn what really happened with the price of the land.
clue: Final report: Peter told her the feet of those who buried her husband were at the door. Afterward the whole church was affected.
prompt: Solution: What does the text say really happened with Ananias and Sapphira?
options: They had agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord; she also fell down dead and was buried beside her husband, and great fear came upon all the church
Sapphira alone planned the deception, and Ananias knew nothing of it
The apostles wrongly accused them, and the church was ashamed
They returned the hidden money, and the matter was quietly settled
explanation: In Acts 5:9-11 Peter asks Sapphira how they had agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord. She fell down and yielded up the ghost, and the young men carried her forth and buried her by (beside) her husband. Great fear came upon all the church and upon as many as heard these things.
hint: Peter's question shows whether the couple acted alone or jointly.
kjv: Then Peter said unto her, How is it that ye have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? behold, the feet of them which have buried thy husband are at the door, and shall carry thee out. Then fell she down straightway at his feet, and yielded up the ghost: and the young men came in, and found her dead, and, carrying her forth, buried her by her husband. And great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things.
r1_problems: The correct option and the explanation say Sapphira 'was buried by her husband.' In modern English this reads as though Ananias buried her, but he was already dead. The KJV 'buried her by her husband' means the young men buried her beside him. The wording should say 'beside her husband.' The clue, prompt, hint and distractors are otherwise sound.

briefing: On the night of the Passover, Jesus sat at the table with his twelve disciples and announced that one of them would betray him. Using the accounts in Matthew 26 and John 13, trace how the agreement was made, how the betrayer was revealed at the table, and what sign was finally used to deliver Jesus over.
clue: A record from the chief priests' meeting: one of the twelve came asking, 'What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you?' A sum was agreed upon.
prompt: For what price did Judas Iscariot covenant with the chief priests?
options: Thirty pieces of silver
Fifty shekels of gold
A field outside Jerusalem
Three hundred pence
explanation: Judas went to the chief priests and 'they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver,' after which he sought opportunity to betray Jesus (Matthew 26:14-16).
hint: The sum was a number of pieces of a precious metal, but not gold.
kjv: Then one of the twelve, called Judas Iscariot, went unto the chief priests, And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver. And from that time he sought opportunity to betray him.
r1_problems: The hint calls silver a 'common metal' and says the coins were 'counted out'. Neither is in the cited text, and silver is a precious metal, so the hint is slightly inaccurate. The answer, options, clue and explanation are sound.

briefing: Case file: The Prisoner Who Walked Free. Peter has been locked in a heavily guarded prison by King Herod, yet by morning he is gone and the soldiers cannot account for him. Investigate the evidence recorded in Acts 12 to discover how the prisoner walked free.
clue: Scene evidence: A light shined in the prison, Peter's chains fell off from his hands, and he and the angel passed the first and the second ward.
prompt: What happened when Peter and his escort reached the iron gate leading to the city?
options: It opened to them of his own accord
Peter broke the lock with his chains
A sympathetic guard unlocked it
They climbed over it with a rope
explanation: Acts 12:10 says the iron gate that leads to the city opened to them of his own accord. Then they passed through one street, and the angel departed from Peter.
hint: No human hand is mentioned at the gate.
kjv: And, behold, the angel of the Lord came upon him, and a light shined in the prison: and he smote Peter on the side, and raised him up, saying, Arise up quickly. And his chains fell off from his hands. And the angel said unto him, Gird thyself, and bind on thy sandals. And so he did. And he saith unto him, Cast thy garment about thee, and follow me. And he went out, and followed him; and wist not that it was true which was done by the angel; but thought he saw a vision. When they were past the first and the second ward, they came unto the iron gate that leadeth unto the city; which opened to them of his own accord: and they went out, and passed on through one street; and forthwith the angel departed from him.
r1_problems: The clue adds a speculative detail: 'Witnesses inside the prison would have seen a light' is not in the text, and it sits awkwardly with the context, where Peter's guards were asleep or unaware (v6, v18). The text says only that 'a light shined in the prison,' not specifically in the cell. 'Chains were found fallen' also implies a later discovery that the text does not record. The question, answer, explanation and hint are accurate.

case_title: The Plot Against the Queen's People
briefing: In the court of king Ahasuerus at Shushan, a royal decree has gone out to destroy every Jew in the empire on a single appointed day, and the queen herself is secretly one of the people marked for death. Investigate Esther 3-7 to trace who set the plot in motion, how it was arranged, and how it was finally exposed.
clue: In the first month, Nisan, in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus, Pur (the lot) was cast before Haman from day to day and from month to month until it settled on a particular month.
prompt: To which month did the lot, called Pur, fall for carrying out the plot?
options: The first month, Nisan
The third month, Sivan
The twelfth month, Adar
The tenth month, Tebeth
explanation: They cast 'Pur, that is, the lot, before Haman from day to day, and from month to month, to the twelfth month, that is, the month Adar' (Esther 3:7).
hint: The lot was cast before Haman in Nisan, but it did not settle on that month.
kjv: In the first month, that is, the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus, they cast Pur, that is, the lot, before Haman from day to day, and from month to month, to the twelfth month, that is, the month Adar. And Haman said unto king Ahasuerus, There is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed among the people in all the provinces of thy kingdom; and their laws are diverse from all people; neither keep they the king’s laws: therefore it is not for the king’s profit to suffer them. If it please the king, let it be written that they may be destroyed: and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver to the hands of those that have the charge of the business, to bring it into the king’s treasuries. And the king took his ring from his hand, and gave it unto Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the Jews’ enemy. And the king said unto Haman, The silver is given to thee, the people also, to do with them as it seemeth good to thee.
r1_problems: The answer is correct and directly stated in Esther 3:7. However, the clue invents a 'record recovered from Haman's chambers', which Scripture never mentions. The hint ('ran on until the last month of the year') effectively gives away the answer, since only one option is the twelfth month. The distractor name 'Tisri' is not a KJV month name (the KJV calls the seventh month Ethanim). A KJV-attested name such as Tebeth (Esther 2:16) is better.

case_title: The Plot Against the Queen's People
briefing: In the court of king Ahasuerus at Shushan, a royal decree has gone out to destroy every Jew in the empire on a single appointed day, and the queen herself is secretly one of the people marked for death. Investigate Esther 3-7 to trace who set the plot in motion, how it was arranged, and how it was finally exposed.
clue: Overheard at Haman's house after the queen's banquet: his wife and friends urged him to have a gallows made, and on the morrow to speak to the king that Mordecai might be hanged on it.
prompt: How high did Zeresh and Haman's friends say the gallows should be made?
options: Twenty cubits
A hundred cubits
Thirty cubits
Fifty cubits
explanation: Zeresh his wife and all his friends said, 'Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high,' and 'he caused the gallows to be made' (Esther 5:14).
hint: The same figure appears again when a chamberlain points out the gallows in Haman's house.
kjv: Then went Haman forth that day joyful and with a glad heart: but when Haman saw Mordecai in the king’s gate, that he stood not up, nor moved for him, he was full of indignation against Mordecai. Nevertheless Haman refrained himself: and when he came home, he sent and called for his friends, and Zeresh his wife. And Haman told them of the glory of his riches, and the multitude of his children, and all the things wherein the king had promoted him, and how he had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king. Haman said moreover, Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and to morrow am I invited unto her also with the king. Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate. Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made.
r1_problems: Minor: the clue says the structure was to be built 'before morning', which the text does not state. Esther 5:14 says only 'Let a gallows be made… and to morrow speak thou unto the king.' The clue also softens the purpose to 'ask the king about Mordecai', when the text says Haman was to ask that Mordecai be hanged. The hint correctly reflects Esther 7:9, where Harbonah, a chamberlain, mentions the gallows fifty cubits high.

intro: Jesus went out of the house, sat by the sea side, and because great multitudes gathered, he entered a ship and taught the people on the shore in parables (Matthew 13:1-3). He later explained the parable of the sower to his disciples (Matthew 13:18).
prompt: In his explanation, what does Jesus say happens when someone hears the word of the kingdom and understands it not?
options: He receives it with joy for a while
The care of this world chokes it
The wicked one catches away what was sown in his heart
He bears fruit an hundredfold
explanation: Matthew 13:19 says that when one hears and understands not, "then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart," which is the seed by the way side.
hint: Think of the seed that fell by the way side, where the fowls came and devoured it.
kjv: When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side.

reading_text.text: The same day went Jesus out of the house, and sat by the sea side. And great multitudes were gathered together unto him, so that he went into a ship, and sat; and the whole multitude stood on the shore. And he spake many things unto them in parables, saying, Behold, a sower went forth to sow; And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up: Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth: And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away. And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them: But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold. Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.

Hear ye therefore the parable of the sower. When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side. But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it; Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended. He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful. But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.

r1_problems: The hint says the seed 'never got into the soil at all', which the text does not state. Matthew 13:4 says only that the seeds 'fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up', and verse 19 even speaks of what 'was sown in his heart'. The hint should stick to the text's wording. Separately, the intro cites 13:18 for the explanation being given to the disciples; the disciples are named in 13:10, but this is a minor contextual point.

parable_title: The Mustard Seed and the Leaven
intro: Sitting in a ship by the sea, Jesus taught great multitudes gathered on the shore, speaking 'many things unto them in parables' (Matthew 13:1-3). These two short parables were spoken to that multitude (Matthew 13:34).
prompt: In the second parable, how many measures of meal did the woman hide the leaven in?
options: Two
Seven
Three
Ten
explanation: The woman 'hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened' (Matthew 13:33).
hint: It is a small number, and the woman kept the leaven in the meal 'till the whole was leavened.'
kjv: Another parable spake he unto them; The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.

reading_text.text: Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof. Another parable spake he unto them; The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened. All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables; and without a parable spake he not unto them: That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world.

r1_problems: The hint ('one more than a pair') gives away the answer outright, since only 'Three' fits, so it no longer works as a hint. Everything else is accurate: the answer, the explanation and the intro context (Matthew 13:1-3 and 13:34).

intro: This parable is the closing illustration of the Sermon on the Mount, which Jesus taught after he "went up into a mountain" and his disciples came to him while the multitudes gathered (Matthew 5:1-2). When he finished, "the people were astonished at his doctrine" (Matthew 7:28).
prompt: When Jesus ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine. What reason does the narrator give for their astonishment?
options: For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes
For he had healed many of their sick that day
For he spoke to them only in parables
For he taught them in the synagogue on the sabbath
explanation: The narrator records that "the people were astonished at his doctrine: For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes" (Matthew 7:28-29).
hint: Read the two verses immediately following the parable.
kjv: And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine: For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.

reading_text.text: Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock. And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell: and great was the fall of it. And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine: For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.

r1_problems: The intro already quotes 'the people were astonished at his doctrine' (Matthew 7:28). That gives away the first half of the answer and makes option 0 trivially identifiable without reading. There is no intro field to fix, so the prompt now asks only for the narrator's reason, with new options to match. Minor: the intro's 'while the multitudes gathered' loosely paraphrases 'seeing the multitudes' (Matthew 5:1).

intro: Jesus told this parable to His disciples right after Peter asked, "Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee; what shall we have therefore?" and Jesus answered that "many that are first shall be last; and the last shall be first" (Matthew 19:27-30). The parable opens with "For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder" (Matthew 20:1), illustrating that saying.
prompt: What wage did the householder agree to pay the labourers he hired early in the morning?
options: A penny a day
Two pence a day
A talent for the season
A share of the vintage
explanation: The householder "agreed with the labourers for a penny a day" and sent them into his vineyard (Matthew 20:1-2).
hint: It was a single coin for the day, agreed before any work began.
kjv: For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard. And when he had agreed with the labourers for a penny a day, he sent them into his vineyard.

reading_text.text: For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard. And when he had agreed with the labourers for a penny a day, he sent them into his vineyard. And he went out about the third hour, and saw others standing idle in the marketplace, And said unto them; Go ye also into the vineyard, and whatsoever is right I will give you. And they went their way. Again he went out about the sixth and ninth hour, and did likewise. And about the eleventh hour he went out, and found others standing idle, and saith unto them, Why stand ye here all the day idle? They say unto him, Because no man hath hired us. He saith unto them, Go ye also into the vineyard; and whatsoever is right, that shall ye receive. So when even was come, the lord of the vineyard saith unto his steward, Call the labourers, and give them their hire, beginning from the last unto the first.

And when they came that were hired about the eleventh hour, they received every man a penny. But when the first came, they supposed that they should have received more; and they likewise received every man a penny. And when they had received it, they murmured against the goodman of the house, Saying, These last have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day. But he answered one of them, and said, Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny? Take that thine is, and go thy way: I will give unto this last, even as unto thee. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good? So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.

r1_problems: The hint calls the penny a 'small coin', which the text does not say. The KJV 'penny' (a denarius) was a full day's agreed wage, so 'small' adds an outside judgment and could mislead. Everything else is accurate.
